# Population-level prevalence and risk of oral HPV infection with or without HPV vaccination

**Authors:** Morgan C Byrd; Alexandra E Hunter; Osayamen Atekha; Rebecca Zasloff; Rong Jiang; Melissa C White; Eric Adjei Boakye; Tammara L Watts; Nosayaba Osazuwa-Peters

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Head and Neck Surgery & Communication Sciences, Duke University School of Medicine, Durham, NC, USA | bDuke University School of Medicine, Durham, NC, USA | cMedical College of Georgia, Augusta, GA, USA | dUniversity of California San Francisco (UCSF), San Francisco, CA, USA | eDepartment of Public Health Sciences, Henry Ford Health System, Detroit, MI, USA | fDepartment of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, Henry Ford Health System, Detroit, MI, USA | gDuke Cancer Institute, Duke University, Durham, NC, USA | hDepartment of Population Health Sciences, Duke University School of Medicine, Durham, NC, USA | iDuke Global Health Institute, Durham, NC, USA

## Abstract

Human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common sexually transmitted infection in the U.S. and the primary cause of multiple anogenital and oropharyngeal cancers. Although HPV vaccination is effective, uptake remains suboptimal and disparities persist. We analyzed nationally representative data from NHANES (2009–2016) to characterize HPV vaccination trends and vaccine-targeted (VT) oral HPV prevalence among adults 18–64 y, with emphasis on vaccine-eligible adults aged 18–26. Weighted prevalence estimates and survey-weighted logistic regression assessed associations between VT oral HPV and vaccination status, sex, race/ethnicity, smoking, alcohol use, and number of lifetime oral sex partners. Latent class analysis (LCA) identified behavioral-risk profiles associated with VT oral HPV. Among 12,479 adults, the weighted prevalence of VT oral HPV infection was 1.9% (95% CI: 1.6–2.2%), higher in males and those reporting smoking, alcohol use, or multiple oral sex partners. Prevalence increased with age, from 1.4% in adults aged 18–26 y to 2.4% in those aged 45–64. Non-Hispanic White participants reported the highest vaccination uptake but the largest sex disparity. Among vaccine-eligible adults, unvaccinated individuals had significantly higher odds of VT oral HPV compared with vaccinated peers (aOR = 4.21, 95% CI: 1.14–15.56). LCA identified five behavioral-risk classes; profiles with low vaccination probability and high oral sex exposure showed the highest VT oral HPV prevalence. HPV vaccination is associated with lower odds against VT oral HPV, yet behavioral exposures remain key contributors to infection risk. Strengthening early vaccination, improving equitable access, and addressing high-risk behaviors may be important strategy components to reduce HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancers.

KEYWORDS: Human papillomavirus viruses, oral HPV, HPV prevalence, HPV vaccination, latent class analysis

## Introduction

Human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common sexually transmitted infection in the United States, affecting an estimated 80 million individuals, with particularly high prevalence among adolescents.1 Persistent infection with oncogenic HPV strains can lead to malignant transformation2,3 and is a well-established etiologic factor of cervical, anal, penile, vulvar, vaginal, and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC).4–6 Historically, cervical cancer accounted for most HPV-associated malignancies; however, over the past four decades, the incidence of HPV-related OPSCC has increased by more than 225%.7–11 As cervical cancer incidence continues to decline due to effective screening and early detection,12 OPSCC has now surpassed cervical cancer as the most common HPV-associated malignancy in the United States.6,13 Unlike cervical cancer, no screening modality exists for OPSCC, making prevention reliant on reducing oral HPV infection.

The development of prophylactic HPV vaccines represents a major advancement in cancer prevention. Landmark clinical trials of the quadrivalent and bivalent HPV vaccines demonstrated near-complete efficacy in preventing persistent infection and precancerous lesions caused by high-risk HPV-16 and HPV-18.14–17 These findings led to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval of the first HPV vaccine (Gardasil) in 2006 for females aged 9–26 y and in 2009 for males. The current 9-valent HPV vaccine (Gardasil 9), approved in 2014, protects against nine oncogenic HPV types and prevents over 90% of HPV infections in a cost-effective manner.18–21 The U.S. Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommends a two-dose series for individuals initiating vaccination before age 15, and a three-dose series for those starting later.22 Timely initiation and completion are essential for achieving optimal immune response.23 In 2020, the FDA expanded Gardasil 9’s indication to include prevention of HPV-related oropharyngeal and other head and neck cancers, further emphasizing the vaccine’s potential to curb the growing burden of HPV-associated OPSCC.7

Despite strong evidence of vaccine efficacy and herd immunity benefits, HPV vaccination uptake in the U.S. remains suboptimal. As of 2022, fewer than 39% of youth aged 9–17 had received at least one dose, and among adults aged 27–45, fewer than one in six report vaccination.24–27 Persistent disparities remain: boys are less likely than girls to initiate vaccination; Hispanic adolescents have lower coverage than their non-Hispanic peers; and uninsured youth and those from families with lower educational attainment are less likely to be vaccinated.24,25 These trends parallel survival differences in HPV-associated cancers, where Black and Hispanic populations experience worse outcomes despite the generally favorable prognosis of HPV-positive tumors.28,29 Immunocompromised individuals, including people living with HIV, are also at higher risk of persistent HPV infection and malignant progression.30

Little is known about how the FDA’s expanded vaccine indication has influenced vaccination uptake or oral HPV prevalence. The impact of this policy change on future OPSCC trends also remains unclear. With OPSCC incidence continuing to rise, the potential benefits of expanded vaccine eligibility will not be realized without improvements in vaccine uptake. At the same time, vaccine hesitancy–driven by political polarization, misinformation on social media, and concerns about safety–continues to impede progress.31

To address these gaps, we analyzed a population-level dataset to evaluate HPV vaccine uptake by sex and race/ethnicity, and to characterize oral HPV prevalence by vaccination status, sex, race/ethnicity, smoking history, alcohol consumption, and lifetime number of oral sex partners among U.S. adults. By examining these patterns in the context of the FDA’s expanded vaccine indication and shifting vaccination behaviors, this study provides timely insights into the epidemiologic drivers of oral HPV infection and identifies opportunities for targeted prevention of HPV-associated OPSCC.

## Methods

### Study population

We analyzed publicly available data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) for adults ages 18–64 y from 2009–2016 (n = 12,479). NHANES is a continuous, cross-sectional study started in 1999 by the National Center for Health Statistics, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.32 NHANES collects data biennially and uses a multistage probability sampling approach to represent the civilian, non-institutionalized U.S. population. Participants complete a household interview to provide demographic and behavioral information and then are invited to participate in a health examination conducted at a Mobile Examination Center (MEC), where biological samples are collected. Informed consent is obtained prior to both the household interview and the health examination. For this analysis, we combined the 2009–2010, 2011–2012, 2013–2014, and 2015–2016 cycles, applying the provided 2-year MEC weights to calculate an 8-year survey weight (MEC 2-year weight/4 for the number of 2-year cycles).33

### Oral HPV and HPV vaccination status

Oral HPV infection was determined using the oral rinse sample collected at the MEC and analyzed for 38 HPV genotypes, including oncogenic and non-oncogenic types, using the Roche Linear Array HPV Genotyping Test methods previously described.11 Samples were classified as “positive,” “negative,” “not evaluated,” or “missing”; those that were not tested or missing were excluded from this analysis. HPV was assessed as vaccine-targeted (VT) oral HPV, including types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58.34 HPV vaccination was self-reported, and participants were asked if they ever received one or more doses. In the 2009–2010, HPV vaccination questions were administered only to female participants aged nine years and greater, as male vaccination had not yet received FDA approval. Beginning in the 2011–2012 cycle, both males and females aged nine years and older were asked about HPV vaccine receipt. Only data on adults 18 and older are publicly available and were included in this analysis.

### Other covariates

Demographic and behavioral variables were obtained from the household interview including sex, race/ethnicity, smoking history, alcohol consumption, and sexual behaviors. Sex was reported as “male” or “female.” Race/ethnicity was self-reported: participants were asked to select a category that best described their race and whether they were of Hispanic/Latino origin. NHANES then grouped participants into a combined category that includes individuals who reported: Non-Hispanic White, Non-Hispanic Black, Mexican American, Other Hispanic, and Other/Multi-Racial. These categories were maintained for table reporting and HPV-vaccination prevalence estimates. However, they were collapsed into Non-Hispanic White, Non-Hispanic Black, and Other (including Mexican American, Other Hispanic, and Other/Multi-Racial) for modeling. Self-reported lifetime smoking history was assessed as a binary variable, defined by whether participants had smoked equal and greater than 100 cigarettes over their lifetime. Alcohol consumption was assessed based on self-report of having consumed ≥12 alcoholic beverages within a one-year period. These measures reflect NHANES collection of lifetime behaviors rather than current use only. The number of lifetime oral sex partners was obtained from the sexual behaviors questionnaire. The total number of lifetime oral sex partners (male and/or female) was calculated and then categorized into 0, 1, 2–5, 6–15, and 16 or more based on prior analyses.35

### Statistical analysis

We calculated weighted prevalence estimates of VT oral HPV for all adults (n = 12,479) and for vaccine-eligible adults aged 18–26 y (n = 2,947). Among vaccine-eligible adults, weighted HPV vaccination prevalence was estimated across NHANES cycle and by sex and race/ethnicity. These estimates and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were plotted to visualize trends. Differences in vaccination prevalence across NHANES cycle, sex, and race/ethnicity were evaluated using survey-weighted Rao-Scott chi-squared tests. Survey-weighted logistic regression was used to assess temporal trends across NHANES cycles, with significance evaluated using Wald tests adjusted for sex and race/ethnicity. Unless otherwise specified, all reported prevalence values are weighted.

We then fit a survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression model to estimate adjusted odds ratios (aORs) for VT oral HPV by vaccination status, adjusting for sex, race/ethnicity, lifetime smoking history, alcohol consumption, and number of lifetime oral sex partners within the cohort of vaccine-eligible adults. These covariates were selected as they are known risk factors for oral HPV. We assessed model diagnostics for all regression analyses. Multicollinearity among covariates was evaluated using variance inflation factors (VIF). A sensitivity analysis fit the same model with number of doses of the vaccine received as the primary predictor instead of binary vaccination status.

To complement the above hypothesis-driven approach, we conducted a latent class analysis (LCA) to identify unobserved subgroups of participants with similar demographic and behavioral patterns. LCA was performed using the “poLCA” package in R, testing models with 2–5 classes. Each model was estimated with 10 random starting values (nrep = 10) and up to 5,000 iterations (maxiter = 5000) per replication. A sensitivity analysis was performed by increasing the random starting values (nrep = 50) to ensure model stability. The solution with the highest log-likelihood was retained for interpretation. Model selection was guided by fit statistics, specifically the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), and entropy; the solution with the lowest AIC and BIC values and the highest entropy were selected as the optimal number of latent classes (Supplemental Materials). Participants were assigned to the class with the highest posterior probability. The latent class analysis was conducted as an unweighted, model-based clustering approach, as standard implementation of “poLCA” does not incorporate complete survey weights during class enumeration.

We then estimated survey-weighted prevalence of VT oral HPV by class membership and conducted survey-weighted logistic regression to estimate odds ratios for VT oral HPV by class. This approach allowed identification of high-risk profiles while accounting for the co-occurrence of multiple predictors. Because our implementation of latent class was conducted using complete cases, the sample-size included 2,384 after excluding those missing smoking history (n = 370) and alcohol consumption (n = 321) data. To evaluate potential selection bias introduced by this restriction, we compared included and excluded participants using survey-weighted chi-squared tests for key demographic and outcome variables (Supplemental Materials). All analyses were performed using R version 4.4.2 and accounted for NHANES complex survey design using the “survey” package, incorporating sampling weights, clustering, and stratification. This data is publicly available and deidentified and was thus exempt from review by the Institutional Review Board.

## Results

### Study population and weighted prevalence of VT oral HPV

A total of 12,479 adults aged 18–64 y with available oral HPV and vaccination data were included in the analytical sample, of whom 2,947 were vaccine-eligible adults aged 18–26 y (Figure 1). When applying survey weights, the overall weighted prevalence of VT oral HPV infection among U.S. adults was 1.9% (95% CI: 1.6–2.2%) (Table 1). VT oral HPV prevalence was higher among males (3.6%; 95% CI: 3–4.3%) than females (0.7%; 95% CI: 0.5–1%) and increased with age, ranging from 1.4% in those aged 18–26 y (95% CI: 0.8–1.9%) to 2.4% among adults aged 45–64 y (95% CI: 1.8–3%). Prevalence was 2.0% among non-Hispanic White adults (95% CI: 1.6–2.5%), 2.2% among non-Hispanic Black adults (95% CI: 1.5–2.9%), and 1.5% among adults of other racial/ethnic groups (95% CI: 1.1–1.9%). Individuals who reported smoking 100 cigarettes or more in their lifetime (2.9%; 95% CI: 2.3–3.6%) or consuming 12 or more alcoholic drinks in one year (2.2%; 95% CI: 1.8–2.6%) had higher prevalence compared with those who smoked and drank less frequently or not at all. Prevalence also increased with number of lifetime oral sex partners, reaching 9.1% among those reporting 16 or more partners (95% CI: 6–12.1%). Among vaccine-eligible adults, similar trends were observed, with higher prevalence among males, smokers, and those reporting multiple oral sex partners.

### HPV vaccination trends

We visualized the weighted prevalence of HPV vaccination across NHANES cycles by sex and race/ethnicity (Figure 2). Across all survey cycles and racial/ethnic groups, females consistently had higher vaccination uptake than males. In both sexes, vaccination prevalence increased across survey cycles, with minor exceptions – Mexican American females in 2011–2012 and other Hispanic males in 2015–2016 showed small decreases. Non-Hispanic White participants had the highest vaccination prevalence overall, though also the largest sex differences within each cycle. Non-Hispanic Black, Mexican American, Other Hispanic, and Other/Multi-Racial participants had comparable uptake within sex and across cycles. Using Rao-Scott chi-squared tests, significant differences in vaccination prevalence were independently found across cycles (p < .0001), sex (p < .0001), and race/ethnicity (p = .0003), indicating meaningful variation in vaccination uptake across all sociodemographic strata. In an adjusted survey-weighted logistic regression controlling for sex and race/ethnicity, HPV vaccination demonstrated a significant increasing linear trend across NHANES cycles (OR per cycle = 1.34, F = 71.17, p < .0001).

### Survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression

Among vaccine-eligible adults, unvaccinated individuals had significantly higher odds of VT oral HPV compared to vaccinated individuals (aOR = 4.21, 95% CI: 1.14–15.56) (Figure 3). A strong dose-response was observed with the number of lifetime oral sex partners: compared to individuals with none, those reporting 6–15 partners (aOR = 5.3, 95% CI: 1.02–27.4) and 16 or more partners (aOR = 30.51, 95% CI: 5.09–182.89) had higher odds of infection. Although not statistically significant, higher odds of VT oral HPV were also observed among males (aOR = 2.29, 95% CI: 0.89–5.91), individuals who smoked ≥100 cigarettes in their lifetime (aOR = 1.87, 95% CI: 0.92–3.8), and those who consumed ≥12 alcoholic drinks in one year (aOR = 1.73, 95% CI: 0.43–6.92), after adjustment for vaccination status and all other covariates in the model. Differences by race/ethnicity were also noted, with elevated odds among Non-Hispanic Black participants and lower odds among participants of other races, compared with Non-Hispanic White individuals, though these differences were not statistically significant. Model diagnostics are reported in the Supplemental Materials. A sensitivity analysis evaluating the number of vaccine doses received as the primary predictor identified similar magnitudes and direction of effects for each covariate (Supplemental Materials), with the lowest odds observed among those who received 1 dose (aOR = 1.65E-07, 95% CI 7.08E-08–3.85E-07) compared to unvaccinated individuals.

### Latent class analysis

Latent class analysis identified a five-class solution as optimal (AIC: 22,678.94; BIC: 22,990.87; entropy: 0.61). Entropy indicated moderate class separation, suggesting some uncertainty in class assignment, as expected in behavioral latent class models. Classes differed by HPV vaccination status, sex, race/ethnicity, lifetime smoking, alcohol consumption, and number of lifetime oral sex partners (Figure 4). Across classes, the probability of HPV vaccination ranged from approximately 34% to 54%, indicating relatively similar vaccine coverage. In contrast, sex, smoking history, alcohol consumption, and the oral sex exposure showed greater variation and were most influential in differentiating classes.

*Figure 4.: Probabilities of each response level for six predictors of vaccine-targeted oral HPV infection (vaccination status, lifetime number of oral sex partners, alcohol consumption, lifetime smoking, sex, and race/ethnicity) by latent class (optimal n = 5). Percentages indicate the probability of each category within a latent class.*

Survey-weighted prevalence of VT oral HPV varied across latent class profiles. Class 1 had 0% VT oral HPV prevalence, moderate HPV vaccination probability (34%), predominately male (68%), high lifetime smoking (96%), moderate alcohol use (86%), and moderate oral sex exposure. Class 2 had VT oral HPV prevalence of 2.3%, very low vaccination probability (4%), moderate smoking (62%), high alcohol use (88%), and moderate oral sex exposure. Class 3 had low VT oral HPV prevalence (0.4%), higher vaccination probability (54%), predominately male (87%), moderate smoking (86%), high alcohol use (81%), and moderate-to-high oral sex exposure. Class 4 had oral HPV prevalence of 0.1%, lower vaccination probability (26%), predominately male (58%), very high smoking (99%), moderate alcohol use (73%), and low oral sex exposure. Class 5 had the highest VT oral HPV prevalence of 3.6%, slightly lower vaccination probability (30%), predominately male (65%), low lifetime smoking (21%), very high alcohol use (93%), and high lifetime oral sex exposure. Overall, higher vaccination coverage, as seen in Classes 1 and 3, were associated with lower VT oral HPV prevalence, while behavioral factors such as oral sex exposure and alcohol use may contribute to differences in infection risk in this cohort.

### Associations between class membership and VT oral HPV

Survey-weighted logistic regression examined the association between latent class membership and VT oral HPV positivity. Participants in Class 5 had the highest predicted odds of HPV positivity (β = 16.12), followed by Class 2 (β = 15.66), Class 3 (β = 13.80), and Class 4 (β = 12.64) when compared to Class 1. These findings align with both the descriptive results and the hypothesis-driven regression, suggesting that classes characterized by lower HPV vaccination probability and greater oral sex exposure, notably Classes 2 and 5, had the highest likelihood of HPV positivity. These patterns should be interpreted cautiously given the data-driven nature of latent class analysis.

## Discussion

This study provides updated, population-level evidence on HPV vaccination uptake and oral HPV prevalence among U.S. adults, illustrating the evolving epidemiology across four NHANES cycles (2009–2016). We demonstrate that HPV vaccination is associated with lower prevalence of VT oral HPV infections, as reflected by the strong inverse association observed in our analysis. These findings align with existing literature documenting the vaccine’s strong efficacy against targeted strains.18–21,23,28 Although our data precede the FDA’s 2020 expansion of vaccine indications to include prevention of oropharyngeal cancers, they provide a critical baseline for understanding HPV epidemiology during the decade leading up to this policy change.7

Two notable trends emerge from our analysis. First, a marked increase in HPV vaccine uptake among young adults aged 18–26 y throughout 2009–2016. Second, during the same period, we observed a decline in oral HPV prevalence among vaccine-eligible adults. Together, these findings suggest that current HPV vaccination rates may be associated with the measurable reductions in oral HPV infection, earlier than some projections had anticipated.36 These results provide compelling real-world evidence of the vaccine’s population-level impact on oral HPV infections during its first decade of implementation.

Prior NHANES-based analyses established post-licensure reductions in genital and oral HPV among adolescents and young adults following the introduction of the quadrivalent vaccine; however, most of these studies focused primarily on genital HPV outcomes or only captured data prior to 2018.11,36,37 Our study extends these observations by incorporating additional NHANES cycles and demonstrates continued increases in vaccination uptake among young adults alongside declining VT oral HPV prevalence. These patterns support the vaccine’s durable immunogenicity and expanding influence on oral HPV transmission dynamics even before broader age-range eligibility was implemented.

Across survey cycles, both males and females showed increasing vaccination coverage, though females consistently reported higher uptake, consistent with the vaccine’s initial rollout focused on cervical cancer prevention.38 Non-Hispanic White participants reported the highest overall uptake, but interestingly, exhibited the largest sex disparity. In contrast, Non-Hispanic Black, Mexican American, Other Hispanic, and Other/Multi-Racial participants showed steadier increases in uptake with comparatively smaller sex gaps. These patterns indicate that although sex disparities are less pronounced in several racial/ethnic groups, racial/ethnic disparities in overall HPV vaccine uptake remain persistent. Structural barriers to HPV vaccination, including limited access, concerns about safety, cost, perceived risk, and misinformation, remain key drivers of these inequities.39–42 Targeted public health strategies are needed to increase equitable vaccine access and awareness.

Despite gains among younger adults, oral HPV prevalence remained highest among adults aged 45–64 y. However, these age-related patterns should be interpreted with caution, as the may reflect cohort effects rather than aging alone. Individuals in this age group were largely ineligible during the early rollout of HPV vaccination and may have acquired infection prior to vaccine availability, whereas younger cohorts have benefitted from increasing vaccination coverage due to public health initiatives and policy changes, including school entry requirements and the Affordable Care Act.39, 43–47 Consequently, observed differences by age likely represent a combination of cumulative exposure risk and generational differences in vaccination uptake, rather than a purely biological effect of aging. Importantly, our regression and subgroup analyses were restricted to vaccine-eligible adults aged 18–26 y, minimizing potential confounding by age and cohort effects in the primary analytical models. Although our data do not extend to the years following the FDA’s 2020 indication expansion, our findings highlight a substantial unmet prevention need in mid-to-older adults that expanded catch-up vaccination (now recommended through age 45) may help address.

Importantly, vaccination status alone did not fully account for differences observed in oral HPV risk. Our latent class analysis demonstrated that although HPV vaccination probability varied only modestly across classes (approximately 34–54%), behavioral factors – particularly lifetime oral sexual exposure, alcohol consumption, and smoking – exhibited far greater variability and were the primary drivers distinguishing class profiles. The classes with the highest survey-weighted VT oral HPV prevalence (Classes 2 and 5) were characterized by low vaccination probability coupled with high-risk behavioral patterns, including elevated alcohol use and greater lifetime oral sex exposure. In contrast, classes with higher vaccination probabilities and more moderate behavioral profiles (e.g., Classes 1 and 3) showed markedly lower VT oral HPV prevalence. Regression analyses further supported these findings, with individuals in Class 5 exhibiting the highest predicted odds of VT oral HPV positivity, followed by those in Class 2. Together, these results underscore the multifactorial nature of oral HPV acquisition. While HPV vaccination was consistently associated with lower prevalence patterns across latent class profiles, behavioral exposures were also key characteristics distinguishing higher-risk classes. These findings suggest that both vaccination status and behavioral factors co-occur within distinct population profiles, particularly among adults who were not vaccinated during adolescence and may have differing exposure histories.

### Public health implications

Our findings suggest that HPV vaccination was beginning to reshape HPV epidemiology in the U.S. by 2016, with increasing uptake among eligible young adults and concurrent declines in VT oral HPV. Although these data predate the 2020 FDA indication expansion, they provide important contextual evidence consistent with potential population-level impacts of early vaccine uptake on VT oral HPV epidemiology. Sustained promotion of early vaccination, equitable catch-up programs, and behavioral risk-reduction strategies will be essential to maximizing the potential population benefit of HPV vaccination in HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancers.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these results. First, as NHANES is a cross-sectional survey, we are unable to evaluate causality and so the lack of temporally linked vaccination status and infection is also prone to reverse causation. Because latent class analysis is an exploratory approach, the identified classes should not be interpreted as definitive or causal groupings. The observed differences across classes may reflect underlying patterns in this sample and require validation in independent populations. Additionally, as smoking and alcohol were key indicators defining the latent class structure, exclusion of participants with missing data on these variables may introduce selection bias if the missingness was associated with underlying characteristics. While the proportion of missing data was moderate, this limitation, along with the use of an unweighted latent class model, should be considered when interpreting the class-specific estimates and evaluating the generalizability of these findings. Oral HPV was assessed via oral rinse samples, which treat the oral cavity as a single homogenous environment; this sampling approach may introduce measurement error and variability in detection, potentially leading to misclassification of oral HPV status. Self-reported variables are also prone to recall bias and misclassification. However, prior validation studies suggest high concordance between self-reported vaccination and immunization records among young adults.48–50 Any misclassification of vaccination is likely to be non-differential, which would bias associations toward the null. Although we adjusted for key covariates, other measured and unmeasured factors that were not included may confound our findings, such as age at sexual debut, concurrent sexual behaviors, and socioeconomic indicators. Vaccination was evaluated as a binary variable for the LCA and age at vaccination and whether vaccination occurred prior to sexual debut were not evaluated due to substantial missingness. This may limit interpretation of vaccination-related associations and potentially obscure meaningful differences. Participants are eligible for vaccination under 18 y of age; however, this information was not publicly available and therefore, could not be included in this analysis. As our sample size decreased in the vaccine-eligible cohort, this resulted in small counts for certain covariate contributing to wider confidence intervals that limits the precision of these interpretations. Despite these limitations, the consistency of findings across multiple analytic approaches supports the robustness of our conclusions.

## Conclusion

While significant attention is placed on the diagnosis and treatment of oropharyngeal cancer, our findings underscore the importance of prevention-focused strategies. Behavioral factors, including alcohol use and oral sex exposure, along with gaps in HPV vaccination coverage were key characteristics of vaccine-targeted oral HPV infection. Strengthening education around safer sexual practices and addressing vaccine hesitancy may be important components of efforts to improve HPV prevention and reduce the burden of HPV-associated disease in the coming decades.
